sections.h2: No New Hampshire tax on the gain
sections.html:
Selling a house in New Hampshire does not trigger a state tax on your profit. The state taxes no W-2 wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax is repealed.

Three other costs remain. The federal government taxes home-sale profit unless an exclusion covers it, the state takes a transfer tax on the deed, and the town expects its share of property tax at closing. Questions about your own return can go to the Department of Revenue Administration Taxpayer Services Call Center at (603) 230-5920 or to a tax professional. Treat this page as general information.

  • Income tax: none on wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax is repealed
  • Transfer tax: charged on the deed, shared by buyer and seller
  • Federal: capital gain tax on profit beyond the home sale exclusion
  • Town: property tax prorated or paid at closing

sections.h2: The Interest and Dividends Tax is gone
sections.html:
The Interest and Dividends (I&D) Tax applied to interest and dividend income, and it was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024. It never reached the proceeds of a house sale. People confuse it with a capital gains tax because it was New Hampshire's only tax that reached investment income.

Taxable periodI&D Tax rate
Ending before December 31, 20235 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20234 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20243 percent
Beginning after December 31, 2024Repealed

The repeal is covered in Technical Information Release 2025-001, and the law sits in RSA 77 and Rev 900. If you still need to file a final I&D return for an earlier period, file them on Granite Tax Connect.

sections.h2: How does the federal home sale exclusion work?
sections.html:
A seller of a main home can shelter up to $250,000 of profit from federal tax, or up to $500,000 when a married couple files jointly. Two tests apply: ownership and use.

Ownership means the name on the title was yours for at least 24 months during the five years leading up to closing. Use means the house was your residence for at least 24 months inside that same five-year window. The months need not overlap. For a joint return, one spouse can satisfy ownership alone, while both spouses must satisfy use.

  • A second exclusion is generally off the table if you already excluded profit on a different home in the two years before this sale.
  • A Form 1099-S in your mailbox means the sale must be reported, even when every dollar of gain is excludable.
  • Reporting goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D when the rules call for it.
  • Military, Foreign Service and intelligence-community members on qualified extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years.
  • Publication 523 holds the full rules, worksheets and exceptions.

Taking payments over several years through an installment sale does not cost you the exclusion.

sections.h2: Federal rates on gain above the exclusion
sections.html:
Profit on a house owned longer than one year counts as long-term and is taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent for most sellers, depending on taxable income. Owned a year or less, the profit is short-term and is taxed like ordinary pay.

For taxable years beginning in 2025, a single filer pays 0 percent up to $48,350, 15 percent from $48,350 to $533,400, and 20 percent above $533,400. A married couple filing jointly pays 0 percent up to $96,700, 15 percent from $96,700 to $600,050, and 20 percent above $600,050.

Rental history changes things. Any slice of profit traced to unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property is taxed at no more than 25 percent, which matters if you rented the house and wrote off depreciation. Higher earners may owe the net investment income tax as well, and a big profit can mean estimated payments during the year.

If you sell a personal home at a loss, the loss is not tax deductible.

sections.h2: Inherited or improved homes: figuring the gain
sections.html:
Taxable gain equals what the sale brings in, less your adjusted basis. Basis starts with what you paid, rises with improvements that add value, and falls with items like allowable depreciation.

A house that came to you as a gift or an inheritance follows different basis rules, laid out in Publication 551, Basis of Assets. If you inherited, order an appraisal showing the value on the date of death and file it with the estate papers, since your preparer will want it.

  • Improvements: new roof, additions, major systems. Keep receipts.
  • Selling costs: ask your preparer which closing costs reduce the amount realized.
  • Holding period: a house acquired from a decedent has its own holding-period rules, covered in Publication 544.

On the sale itself, New Hampshire charges $0.75 for every $100 of the price, and the buyer and the seller each pay that rate. Where the price is $4,000 or less, each side owes a flat $20 minimum. RSA 78-B and Rev 800 govern it.

Each party purchases stamps at the register of deeds for the county where the house sits, and the register affixes them to the deed at recording.

Paperwork follows within 30 days of recording: the purchaser files form CD-57-P, the seller files CD-57-S, and the Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34) goes to the state. Granite Tax Connect handles both filing and payment.

  • Taxable: sales, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu, sheriff's sale deeds, leases of 99 years or more
  • Exempt: gifts, transfers between spouses under a final divorce decree, corrective deeds, transfers to the state, a county or a municipality, and transfers by devise, intestate succession or a joint tenant's death

sections.h2: Property tax in a New Hampshire sale
sections.html:
RSA 76:2 sets the tax year as April 1 through March 31, with assessments built on the April inventory. The April 1 owner is the name on the bill, and the closing agent divides the year between buyer and seller.

Overdue taxes accrue 8 percent interest (RSA 76:13). Once a municipal tax lien is recorded, RSA 80:69 applies 14 percent a year to it, and any party with a legal interest in the land may redeem before the collector issues a deed. A title company normally pays off the lien out of your sale proceeds.

For city specifics, our Manchester and Nashua guides cover those offices and dates.

sections.h2: Before you sell with a large gain
sections.html:
Settle your basis and your exclusion on paper before signing a contract. Those two figures decide whether federal tax is due at all. A single seller who lived in the house two of the last five years and clears less than $250,000 in profit may owe nothing federally, although some sales must still be reported.

  1. Gather the purchase closing statement and improvement receipts.
  2. Count your months of ownership and residence in the last five years.
  3. Check whether a 1099-S will be issued.
  4. Ask a preparer about estimated tax if a taxable gain is likely.
  5. Budget for the 0.75 percent transfer tax on your side.

Selling for cash leaves the tax rules alone. What it changes is the calendar, so you can line up the day proceeds arrive with any estimated payment your preparer expects. Take your original closing statement, improvement receipts and any tax notices along to that first meeting.

faqs.q: Does New Hampshire have a capital gains tax?
faqs.a: Not on a home sale. The state taxes no W-2 wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax was repealed for periods beginning after December 31, 2024. Federal tax can still apply.

faqs.q: How much profit can I exclude when I sell my house?
faqs.a: Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, provided you owned and lived in the house for at least 24 months of the last five years. A prior exclusion on another home within two years rules it out.

faqs.q: Who pays the New Hampshire real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: The buyer and seller each pay $0.75 per $100 of the price. Transfers through a will, intestate succession or a joint tenant's death are exempt.

faqs.q: Do I report a home sale if I owe no tax?
faqs.a: Yes when a Form 1099-S arrives, even if the gain is fully excludable. Report it as well when part of the gain is taxable.

faqs.q: Can I deduct a loss on my personal home?
faqs.a: No. A loss on personal-use property such as your home is not tax deductible.
